newsitem.title: DUBAI: GOLF-GREEN BEATS ROLE MODEL NORMAN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-GREEN BEATS ROLE MODEL NORMAN.

text.p: When you are ranked 198th in the world you are not expected to beat your role medal, especially when he is world number one Greg Norman.

But that is exactly what 26-year-old Richard Green did at the Dubai Desert Classic on Sunday, defeating Norman and Ian Woosnam in a play-off and leaving other luminaries including Colin Montgomerie and Bernhard Langer in his wake.

The Australian left-hander has always looked up to Norman since watching him win the 1986 British Open at Turnberry just a few months after he failed to capture the U.S. Masters when he famously mishit his approach at the final hole.

"I have the tape of that event when Greg blocked his second shot out to the right and I have replayed it probably 400 times. I keep praying the shot goes right into the hole but the tape doesn't change," he said after his victory on Sunday.
"He's an awesome player and I admire him for what he's done. I aspire to be like him.
"I met him today for the first time in the scorer's box which was just unbelievable. Then to play with him and beat him, well ... ."
Green, a strapping six-footer (1.95 metres?, already shares Norman's love of fast cars.
He regards motor racing as a "serious passion" which he hopes to do as a hobby one day.
He has owned and raced cars and plans to buy another one soon. "But as much of a buzz as that is, I've never had the feeling I had on the golf course today."
He was racing a car a few years ago which spun 360 degrees at 180 kph. "But it finished out on the middle of the track, so I was okay."
Green has always been a left-handed golfer, as was his father George who introduced him to the game when he was six.

The Melbourne native enjoyed a successful youth career representing his state and one of his mentors was Norman Von Nida, who still holds a European Tour record of seven victories in one season, set back in 1947.
"He talks to me about the mental side of the game and takes a keen interest in my progress. He was a gutsy little player and to have that mentality would be great," Green said.
Green, whose wife Anita caddies for him, decided to commit himself to the European Tour after finishing fifth in the Heineken Classic in Perth in January last year.
He paid the fee to become an affiliate member, competed 13 times and made the cut in 10 to earn his full playing card for this year.

His best finish came in a rain-reduced BMW Open in Munich, where he was second, but he considers sixth place in the Loch Lomond Invitational in Scotland a bigger achievement because the field was stronger.
"I want to play the European Tour for the next five years at least, maybe 10. I just want to keep on for as long as possible.
"But I would also like to play on the U.S. Tour, combine them both. I'd like to travel all over the world to play golf, that's my ambition.
"Now that I know I can do this under these circumstances and under the pressure I've put on myself, I know I can be competitive on a world level."
